content: Human African trypanosomiasis, also known as sleeping sickness, is a severe and often fatal disease if left untreated. It predominantly affects individuals in the poorest regions of Africa. Traditional treatments for the disease require several days of intravenous infusions. However, a newer drug, fexinidazole, offers the advantage of oral administration. Another oral drug candidate, acoziborole, is currently under clinical development and will be evaluated in future studies. The objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of currently available drugs for treating second-stage Trypanosoma brucei gambiense trypanosomiasis (gambiense human African trypanosomiasis, or g-HAT). A comprehensive search was conducted on May 14, 2021, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, Embase, and others. Reference lists of included studies were reviewed, and researchers and relevant organizations were contacted to identify eligible studies. Only randomized controlled trials involving adults and children with second-stage g-HAT treated with currently used anti-trypanosomal drugs were included. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed by two reviewers, with a third reviewer acting as an arbitrator if necessary. The included trial reported dichotomous outcomes, which were analyzed using risk ratios (RR) or risk differences (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The review included one trial that compared fexinidazole to the combination therapy of nifurtimox and eflornithine (NECT). This trial was conducted between October 2012 and November 2016 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic, involving 394 participants. The study evaluated both efficacy and safety, with follow-up extending up to 24 months. The trial was judged to have a low risk of bias in all domains except for blinding. Due to differences in administration routes and dosing regimens between the treatment groups, neither participants nor personnel were blinded, leading to a high risk of performance bias. Mortality at 24 months appeared to be higher in the fexinidazole group compared to the NECT group. Specifically, there were 9 deaths out of 264 participants in the fexinidazole group, compared to 2 deaths out of 130 participants in the NECT group (RR 2.22, 95% CI 0.49 to 10.11; low-certainty evidence). Importantly, none of these deaths were attributed to the treatments themselves. Fexinidazole was also associated with a higher likelihood of relapse during follow-up. Fourteen participants in the fexinidazole group relapsed (14/264), whereas no relapses were observed in the NECT group (0/130) at 24 months (RD 0.05, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.08; moderate-certainty evidence). The incidence of serious adverse events at 24 months was uncertain, with 31 serious adverse events reported in the fexinidazole group (31/264) compared to 13 in the NECT group (13/130). Adverse events were common in both treatment groups, affecting 247 out of 264 participants in the fexinidazole group and 121 out of 130 participants in the NECT group. There was no significant difference in the overall frequency of adverse events between the two groups (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.06; moderate-certainty evidence). In conclusion, while oral fexinidazole is significantly easier to administer than conventional treatments, it is associated with higher rates of death and relapse. Despite these concerns, the convenience of an oral treatment option offers substantial benefits, including avoiding hospitalization and intravenous infusions, which may improve treatment adherence.
